notable_absence.finding: Across roughly 30 documented node-level settings and 20+ admin endpoints, only ONE endpoint pair (GET/POST /admin/gc) names a specific Server RBAC role in its 401 response ("the invoking user is not a valid full-admin user") and only ONE setting (completed-stream-size) carries a version gate ("available in Couchbase Server 7.6.4 and later"). Every other endpoint's Security section just says "The Admin API supports admin credentials" without naming a role, and every other setting is undated. Several settings compound this by refusing to explain themselves at all: max-index-api ("This setting is provided for technical support only"), mutexprofile ("Mutex profile. This setting is provided for technical support only") - two properties in the Settings object schema with no behavioral description whatsoever, only a type and, for mutexprofile, a default. An AI agent or reader cannot determine what these settings do from this page, and the page does not point elsewhere for the answer either. A smaller, mechanical version of the same gap: numatrs and cleanupwindow both name 'active transaction records' as the object they configure, but do so with the term embedded inside a Markdown link to a different page's anchor - splitting what would otherwise be a clean, quotable defining sentence in two, which is why this record could evidence atrcollection's tie to n1ql:active-transaction-record but not numatrs's or cleanupwindow's despite the underlying fact being equally true of all three.

cross_component_finding:
This page's own Requests, Statements (Prepared Statements) and Vitals object schemas are the strongest evidence yet for the reconciliation question round 10's intro.json raised but could not resolve on its own page: that /admin/active_requests, /admin/completed_requests, /admin/prepareds and /admin/vitals are REST mirrors of the system:active_requests, system:completed_requests, system:prepareds and system:vitals keyspaces, not separate resources. Concretely: the admin Requests object's clientContextID field cites 'the request-level client_context_id parameter' by name; its cpuTime field cites 'the total sum of execTime across all operators' from the query-plan reference; its scanConsistency field cites 'the query setting Scan Consistency'. These are the exact same fields the monitoring/system-keyspace pages already document for system:active_requests and system:completed_requests, described here from the REST side instead of the SQL++ side. I have again NOT asserted an identity relation (no sentence on this page states 'this endpoint returns the same data as system:X'), for the same reason round 10 gave: the fact is a strong structural inference, not a quoted claim, and the registry still has no predicate for 'same resource, alternate access surface' (round 10 proposed alsoExposedAs/hasAlternativeAccessSurface; neither exists in the current promoted predicate list). This is now evidenced from BOTH directions (the system-keyspace pages and this REST page), which should raise its priority at reconciliation.

Separately: the 'completed' nested Logging Parameters object (n1ql:completed-request-logging-parameters) generalizes far beyond the scalar completed-limit/completed-threshold settings already promoted - it can match on client IP, user name, error number, a LIKE pattern against the statement text, an error count floor, and an arbitrary field:value match against the QUERY PLAN itself ('{"index": "ix1", "#operator": "IntersectScan"}'). That last capability - conditioning what gets logged on the shape of the query PLAN, not just the query's runtime properties - is a real mechanism with no analogue anywhere else I have read in this corpus, and is worth a second look at reconciliation time independent of the settings-mirroring question above.
cross_product_finding: Confirms and extends round 10's finding rather than contradicting it: the Query Admin REST API has NO Capella counterpart at all. cloud/n1ql/ contains no admin.md or equivalent, and every setting this page documents as node-level (auto-prepare, atrcollection, cleanupclientattempts/cleanuplostattempts/cleanupwindow, numatrs, max-parallelism, memory-quota, node-quota, pipeline-batch/cap, scan-cap, txtimeout, use-cbo, use-replica) exists on the Capella side ONLY as a request-level parameter on the query-execution page, never as a node- or cluster-configurable setting. Capella's control plane (capella:management-api, capella:cluster-manager) is the only place node/cluster configuration happens for that product, and it is a wholly separate API from anything modelled in this corpus's n1ql: namespace. The garbage-collector endpoint (n1ql:query-engine-garbage-collector) is the sharpest single illustration: it is a raw Go-runtime operational control exposed directly over HTTP with only a full-admin credential check, a shape of API surface Capella's docs never expose for any service.
